_Logical Positivism_ is a great book. It combines careful attention to archival records, quantitative data, and social context, to tell an incredibly rich story about the rise, and I guess fall, of logical positivism in America. I'm going to recommend it to all my students as crucial background for how philosophy in America got to where it is, and a correction to several popular narratives.

On the data side, this is one of the best examples you'll see of data use that highlights simple understandable statistics. The main statistic the book uses is simply how often different philosophers are mentioned in leading journals. This is not a simple statistic to gather; the amount of data cleaning and analysis to tell when, for example, Roy Wood Sellars is being mentioned and Wilfrid Sellars is being mentioned, is immense. But Verhaegh's team at Tilburg has done a mountain of work to get the data in a form where they can tell, with some confidence, who is being referred to at any point. (They have also made this data freely available to other researchers, for which they deserve a lot of credit.) And now in a book like this claims about changes in philosophy can be backed up with these statistics about how often philosophers are mentioned.

The book also has a number of tables of outliers, e.g., which philosophers are mentioned most often or (relative to expectation), least often in a particular period or in a particular journal. These tables strike me as an absolutely incredible feat. Whenever I build tables of outliers, they just reveal data errors; the most common words are usually bits of meta-data that haven't been cleaned from the text. Of course, it's very easy to understand a table of who was mentioned most or least often, so it's great for the reader to have something like this, but I suspect it was an incredible effort to get the tables to be so useful.

This note will largely be about Verhaegh's discussion of how positivism fed into the rise of analytic philosophy in America, but first I'll briefly discuss two smaller points about the book.

_Logical Positivism_ is primarily a book about a movement within academic institutions. But it isn't entirely about that. The effects of the outside world on positivism are clearly important; we don't get a generation of exiled empiricists without something causing their exile. That is important, and it is discussed well in the book. It isn't just that there were exiles, but who they were, when they came, and where they came from, matter, and we learn a lot more about these questions and why they matter in part 1 of the book.

What's more distinctive, though, is the book's discussion of the effects of positivism on the outside world. In the context of the book, positivism is a radical outside force, that comes in to shake things up, and is opposed by the conservative mainstream. I had a question about a way in which it's possible that the positivists had a lasting and dramatic effect on American education.

Many American schoolchildren these days are taught that there is a very sharp fact/opinion distinction. They get worksheets asking them to classify claims into facts and opinions. These are worksheets, so there is meant to be a right and wrong answer. Whatever the background of these worksheets, which I really don't know, they are positivist in effect. The answers which will be marked correct could be taking straight from _Language, Truth and Logic_. That's to say, they have a very expansive conception of what's 'opinion' as opposed to 'fact', a much more expansive one than many of the American positivists Verhaegh discusses would endorse. The conservative complaints about positivis that Verhaegy discusses in chapter 11, complaints that positivists were separating facts and values, would look really weird to modern American students who have been taught that this distinction is vitally important. Was getting this into the curriculum a success story for positivism, or does it have some other history? I'm not sure, but it feels like an interesting research topic for people who want to look further into the social effects of positivism.

The other small point I want to note is that it's really pleasing to see how central _public_ universities are to the story in _Logical Positivism_. The focus is so often on the famous Ivy League schools, and indeed five of the Ivies are central to Verhaegh's book. But his story also relies on the big public universities too. We see Schlick get a huge audience at Berkeley very early on in the reception of positivism in America, then Feigl gets hired by Iowa and given more resources at Minnesota. Reichenbach, after many challenges, is hired at UCLA. The central university at the end of the narrative, and still the home of the most important positivist archive, is Pitt. After Charles Stevenson is denied tenure at Yale, he gets a permanent home at Michigan, where I'm based. To this day, our most prestigious research prize for graduate students is the Stevenson prize. Stevenson was succeeded at Michigan by Alan Gibbard, so we stayed a center for non-cognitvist meta-ethics for over half a century.

The main thing I want to talk about is the story Verhaegh tells, primarily in chapter 9, of how logical positivism feeds into the spectacular rise of analytic philosophy in America post-WWII. As with all plausible narratives of this rise, Verhaegh's starts with the vexed question of just what this thing, analytic philosophy, is that ended up winning. The story he gives, and which he marshalls excellent evidence for, is that it becomes in effect the merger of the realist and positivist traditions. It's a merger of especially the Cambridge realist tradition with less doctrinaire versions of positivism. 

One really striking thing about the narrative is that the label, 'analytic philosophy', gets used for this would-be coalition before there is any sign of it being a coalition. It's not the only term that gets used; 'scientific' philosophy is just as common. But two projects by Feigl and Sellars seem to be important in the terminological shift. One is the collection _Readings in Philosophical Analysis_ [@FeiglSellars1949]; the other is the founding of the journal _Philosophical Studies_ with the subtitle _An International Journal for Philosophy in the Analytic Tradition_. To a large extent, Feigl and Sellars are inventing this tradition, or perhaps more charitably discovering it, and labeling it. The last is a bit of what we'd now call conceptual engineering. It's massively successful. The forces of 'scientific' philosophy really just run over all before them in the top American universities.

This coalition, the realists and the positivists, looks so unstable. What exactly do they have in common? This is why the definitional question is so hard. The question about commonality can be traced back to the figures who are conscripted into this new tradition. What exactly do Carnap, Moore, and Anscombe, have in common, which they don't also share with Peirce? 

Here Verhaegh also has a good pair of answers. First, what they have in common is a connection to _Russell_. Verhaegh shows the positivists very consciously built a narrative where they were part of a common tradition with Russell, to fend off the charge that they were just a passing fad. Second, there seems to have been something almost deliberate about writing Peirce into the anti-canon.

Let's step back. One simple narrative, already visible in philosophy's self-conception before the rise of positivism, was that there were three primary schools in American philosophy before positivism arrived. These were, in rough order of importance, idealism, pragmatism, and realism [@Morris1935]. There were other smaller schools; in a post-war survey of the state of philosophy Edgar Sheffield @Brightman1947 also lists naturalists, Thomists, personalists and Kantians. But these three were the largest, not least because they had distinctive sub-schools. It helps to start with these three.

The coalition positvists formed with realists was not doctrinal; the positvists did not suddenly go around espousing realist theses. Rather, it was administrative. When philosophy departments were expanding, and there was a lot of post-war expansion, they worked together to make sure positions were set aside for 'scientific'/'analytic' philosophers. But at least during the period analytic philosophy was taking over American philosophy, the positivists were a key part of the coalition. Why did they enter into _this_ coalition, not into a coalition with one of the other major schools? The short answer is that neither of the other coalitions worked.

It would have made sense for pragmatists and positivists to work together. They are both anti-metaphysical. This led people to treat them similarly at the time. Verhaegh quotes Feigl, Morris, Nagel, and Hook as treating them as a pair. If they're different, where do you put Ramsey? Later in life, Ayer does an interview with Bryan McGee [https://philpapers.org/rec/MAGLPA-2, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gBSUMC3CqGg] where he says pragmatism was "very akin to" positivism. 

But this union doesn't work. Verhaegh suggests that it is because the pragmatists were allergic to dichotomies, like the fact/value one, and that seems plausible. There was also a difference in how they treated formalism. It all seems very contingent; it's easy to imagine that if Ramsey had lived he alone might have made the idea of pragmatist positivism work. But he didn't, and this pairing fails; the pragmatists at Columbia become some of the staunchest opponents of positivism.

It's a bit more of a stretch, but you can see how a positivist/idealist coalition could work. Especially in early versions of positivism, they both put conscious experience right at the center. Verhaegh quotes Carnap complaining that people were reading the _Aufbau_ as idealist. While Carnap has a point that that's a misreading, it's not an unintelligible one; there is a synthesis there if someone wants to develop it. But no one did. It's interesting to think about what a philosophical landscape would look like where positivism/idealism vs pragmatism/realism was the main dividing line; perhaps Ayer vs Austin on sense-data would be taught as the central debate in philosophy.^[I've elsewhere argued that the standard stories of the development of analytic philosophy in the actual world don't give enough emphasis to Austin's role - CITE SOAMES BOOK SYMPOSIUM HERE. In this counterfactual he is much more clearly cental.] But that will remain forever a counterfactual; it's not the way philosophy developed.

Instead, we get a positivist/realist coalition. Doctrinally, this seems very unstable. But it gets you two advantages, which Verhaegh stresses. One is that it gets you Russell inside the coalition, without worrying about Russell's changes of views over time. (At least, once he abandons his youthful idealism.) More importantly, it gets you a coalition between philosophers who think that logic and philosophy of science are central to philosophy. Before WWII, you already have @Morris1935 noting how much more comfortable the realists are with mathematical approaches to philosophy than the other schools. This becomes the definining characteristic of this new school; not what answers they give to philosophical questions, but which questions they ask (including questions from philosophy of science), and how they answer them (with tools from mathematics and logic). This turned out to be enough.

Here's my contentious claim. Once that was the dividing line, the victory for the analytics was close to inevitable. We're taught to hate inevitability claims in history, and rightly so. And I do think it was really contingent that this became the dividing line. There are many things that could have happened before WWII that could have upset it. (I already noted Ramsey's survival alone might have complicated the story significantly.) But once those are the sides, I think the analytics have to win. That's for two reasons. 

One is that idealism, especially in America, was dying. And pragmatism was just not strong enough to fight this new coalition on its own. Verhaegh has some damning numbers on this. At the key moment, eleven of Columbia's thirteen faculty were homegrown. If Deweyan pragmatism had really been strong, there would have been graduate students so good you couldn't help hiring them. There weren't.

The bigger reason is that this coalition left the opposing forced hopelessly divided. This is already clear in Verhaegh's telling of the story. At Columbia, the anti-analytics wanted Deweyian pragmatism. At Princeton, they wanted Christian humanism. At Yale, they wanted "space for metaphysics". It's not that surprising that it was hard to put together a unified opposition; if the realists and positivists had to stretch to find things in common, the idealists, pragmatists, Thomsists, etc who opposed them had almost nothing in common except a dislike of the new analytic philosophy. 

When analytic philosophy did face a threat, it was from 'continental philosophy'. Now continental philosophy, like analytic philosophy, covers a multitude of sins. But the advantage each has is that they'll work with a pretty broad range of others under the umbrella, at least for institution building. That's needed to fight a battle like this, and the 1950s anti-analytics didn't have it.

Looking at things from a broadly institutional perspective makes it clear why coalitions, like analytic or contintental philosophy, are going to be well placed to overrun more cohesive schools. As a graduate student, it is much safer to start working in an analytic program, or a continental program, than in a program dedicated to pragmatism, or to Thomism. You can change your mind on key philosophical questions and still feel at home in the program. If the coalition has a big role in hiring, which it does, there is a better chance of a good job at the other end. Both these factors suggest that once a coalition like this gets rolling, it will start sweeping up graduate students. Indeed, that's basically what happened both when the 'analytic' coalition started being formed after WWII, and when the 'continental' coalition started being formed a decade or two later.

There is also an advantage that the hiring end. Academics are always fond of hiring people who share their views, at least about what the interesting questions are, if not always about what the right answers are. (Though the latter happens too, of course.) It's sometimes a challenge, but rarely impossible, to get academics on board with the idea of hiring in an area they are familiar with but don't think much of. It's much harder to get them to hire in areas that they are completely unfamiliar with, which they didn't study in graduate school, and which they don't interact with. One effect of this is that if there are schools of philosophy which are centered around a few universities, then if those are prominent universities, if students elsewhere are not even learning about these schools, then by the time those students are involved in hiring, they will have no interest at all in hiring from those schools.

The coalitional approach avoids this problem. The realist and positivists who were trained by post-war scientific philosophers disagreed on any number of doctrinal points. But they knew about each other, indeed they usually had friends from each side of the various disputes, and they were willing to hire people who looked like their teachers or classmates, even if they had disagreed with those teachers or classmates. (Again, this isn't a point about analytic philosophy; I think you can tell the same story about continental philosophy, and how the existence of continental programs creates philosophers who are willing to hire from the different traditions within continental philosophy.)

So I'll end with a question, one that I guess relates to the discussion of explanation at the end of _Logical Positivism_. I think counterfactuals are crucial to explanation. If we want to explain why analytic philosophy became dominant, we need to ask what the philosophical world would looked like if it never became dominant. My question is, what does that world look like? And how late can it reasonably, feasibly, differ from actual history? My guess is that the deviation from actual history has to come relatively early; by 1950, the outcome is baked in, even though the analytics don't actually take over for several more years. The more expansive analytic programs are going to have an easier job attracting good graduate students, and then those students will be more willing to hire from within this new 'analytic tradition'. I'd like to be convinced I'm wrong; I get nervous with inevitability claims! But this institutional story seems fairly compelling in retrospect.

As hopefully will be clear by now, _Logical Positivism_ is not just full of fascinating details about how positivism developed in America, it tells a fascinating story which opens up new ways of looking at the recent history of philosophy. It's a fantastic book, and I hope it's really widely read.
